pr.title: Add NonNull pattern types
pr.description:
These are the final piece missing for

* https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/136006

We cannot use the previous scheme of using an integer range for raw pointers, as we're not just changing the layout of raw pointers anymore, but also the type representation. And we can't represent "any provenance or NonZero<usize>" natively as patterns. So I created a new `!null` pattern. Since this is all unstable representation stuff for replacing rustc_layout_scalar_range_start with pattern types, the divergence from normal patterns is fine, especially since T-lang seems interested in exploring general negation patterns

r? @BoxyUwU
pr.author: oli-obk

processing.reason: The historical change is confined to MIR validation acceptance, not to any value-producing runtime transformation. In `compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/validate.rs`, the pre-patch omission makes a debug-info field projection whose base is `ty::Pat(base, _)` fall through to `self.fail(...)`, while the patch adds `ty::Pat(base, _) => check_equal(self, location, *base)`. This changes whether the MIR validator accepts or rejects a body; it does not change the runtime value computed by any accepted body. There is no concrete input where the original and transformed program functions both pass Miri and return different numeric/boolean/character values. Constructing a function that merely reports "validator accepts" versus "validator rejects" would model the compile-time validator result with hardcoded booleans rather than encode a historical runtime transformation, and would therefore be a manufactured/ unrelated pair. The PR’s own regression tests are `check-pass`/Miri pass tests (`unsize.rs`, `src/tools/miri/tests/pass/pattern-types.rs`), consistent with a feature-enabling validation fix rather than a runtime miscompilation.

analysis.originalLogic: In the MIR `Validator`/`TypeChecker` visit of debug-info place projections, the projected field type is compared with the type derived from the projection base via `check_equal`. The patch shows that this match needed a `ty::Pat` case. The original validator logic had no such case, so a debug-info projection into a pattern type was not recognized as projecting to the pattern's sole field, whose type is the pattern's base type.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation was to omit the `ty::Pat(base, _)` projection case instead of treating field 0 of a pattern type as its base type and applying `check_equal(self, location, *base)`. In other words, the validator failed to normalize a permitted debug-info field-0 projection through a pattern type to the underlying base type, so the projection was not accepted under the validator's type-consistency rules. This is a feature-enabling correctness fix, not a performance optimization and not a reproduced runtime bug.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR bodies with debug-info place projections whose base type is a pattern type `ty::Pat(base, pat)`, particularly `pattern_type!(*const T is !null)` and wide-pointer forms such as `pattern_type!(*const [u8] is !null)`. The control input is the same projection with the pattern-type wrapper removed and only the base type present. The distinguishing transformation is the presence/absence of the `ty::Pat` node at the projection base, not a change to the projected field index.
analysis.summary: The `Validator` pass must recognize debug-info field projections into pattern types. Layout represents a pattern type as having its base type as field 0, so the validator's projected-field equality check must compare against the base type when the base is `ty::Pat`. The extractable correctness lesson is that a new transparent single-field representation cannot be added only to layout/type lowering; MIR validation also needs an explicit projection case, otherwise debug-info projections through the new representation are not accepted. Source inspection only; no compiler was built and no reproduction is claimed.
analysis.trigger: A debug-info place projection targets field 0 of a value whose type is a pattern type (`ty::Pat`), while MIR validation is checking projection/type consistency.
preconditions: The projection base is a pattern type represented as `ty::Pat(base, pat)`.
The pattern type layout has exactly one field, at offset zero, whose type is the base type.
The projection is emitted for debug info and must be accepted by MIR validation.
The validator is comparing the projected field type with the type implied by the base type.
pitfalls: Do not treat a pattern type as an error/unsupported projection in the validator merely because it is not an ADT; its sole field is its base type.
Do not apply this normalization outside the debug-info projection case without checking the wider typing rules; the invariant here is specifically that pattern types contain their base as field 0.
Do not infer that the validator change is an optimization or that it makes pattern types generally coercible to their base type.
Do not claim the original compiler was executed or that a failure was reproduced; the patch only supplies source evidence.
Do not confuse the syntax with two-word `not null`: the accepted pattern is explicitly `!null`.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a focused MIR-validation regression test that compiles equivalent bodies differing only by wrapping the pointer type in `pattern_type!(*const T is !null)` versus using `*const T`, with debuginfo enabled, and runs the MIR validator. Include a wide-pointer/dyn-unsizing variant such as converting `pattern_type!(*const u32 is !null)` toward `pattern_type!(*const dyn Trait is !null)` so the pattern type participates in a projection/coercion path. The expected invariant is that both the pattern-type and base-only debug-info projections pass validation; a separate negative control should still reject a genuinely type-inconsistent field projection. Treat this as a compile/validation test only, not as evidence of runtime reproduction.
evidence: // Debug info is allowed to project into pattern types
// Pattern types contain their base as their sole field.
// This allows the rest of the compiler to process pattern types just like
// single field transparent Adts, and only the parts of the compiler that
// specifically care about pattern types will have to handle it.
